# Backlog Management for Agent-Executed Work

What changed once agents, rather than people, executed the tickets. Each rule below replaced a
practice that looked reasonable and produced a specific failure.

## 1. The agent never creates a work item

Findings go to a single never-closing findings item as comments. A human owns the backlog.

**What it replaced:** "a TODO identified becomes a ticket immediately." That produced 51
micro-tickets with no feature arc, and a board nobody could plan from. Agents are extremely
good at noticing things and have no sense of proportion about them.

## 2. Size by outcome, not by safety

Three sizes, and the test is whether someone outside the team would notice the result.

| Type | Shape |
|---|---|
| **Feature** | 1 to 5 days, one worktree, one PR |
| **Foundation** | Unblocks dependents, and runs **before** them |
| **Fix batch** | 5 to 15 small items, one PR |

If it cannot be described as a noticeable outcome, it is a checklist line inside another item
or a findings entry. It is not a work item.

**What it replaced:** sizing by "smallest safe isolated change", which optimises for a clean
diff and produces a board of changes nobody asked for.

## 3. Three to five items active, no two sharing a module

Module-disjointness is the mechanism that makes parallel worktrees safe. Declare a module field
on every item and enforce it at selection.

Name your shared files explicitly and admit **one** active item that touches them, whatever the
others declare in scope. Typical shared files: application entry point, DI registration, schema
convergence check, migrations index, shared config. Anything that adds a table or a route
touches these.

## 4. Every item carries the four-section contract

`Outcome`, `Acceptance criteria`, `Scope -- modules and files in play`,
`Explicitly out of scope`, plus `Dependencies` and `Notes`.
See `template-issue-work-item.md`.

An item missing `Acceptance criteria` or `Scope` is **not ready**. Ask the human to fill it in
rather than inventing it. This is the single highest-value rule in the kit: the two enforcement
skills bind to those headings literally, so an item without them silently runs ungated.

## 5. Readiness is the body, not the column

A `feature` label does not mean ready. A `Ready` status does not mean ready. Readiness is:
sections present, criteria verifiable, no open `Blocked by:`, no unresolved "decide before
build" note. Check the body every time.

## 6. Severity judgements the board does not carry

Any judgement your board has no field for becomes a per-item judgement at selection time, and
you must write down the signals that trigger it. Example from a regulated domain: "could this
change a number that reaches a printed, audited certificate?" Strong signals were the module
value and any mention of a calculation, tolerance, limit, unit, rounding rule, classification
boundary, or template formula.

Two properties matter for any such judgement:

- **It routes something**: the session model, whether a plan gate is mandatory, how much review
  the change gets.
- **It follows the change, not the item.** A session that discovers mid-work that its fix
  touches the sensitive area is in that category from that moment, brief notwithstanding.

Where possible make it a label so it becomes mechanical instead of remembered.

## 7. Platform facts worth knowing

Jira + Bitbucket (the primary stack): see `platform-jira-bitbucket.md`, which carries the
field conventions, the comment-only rule for agents, JQL queries, and the Bitbucket PR notes.

GitHub Issues variant:

| Fact | Consequence |
|---|---|
| `gh issue comment` appends, it does not replace the body | Safe for an agent to write. Tools that replace an entire body on every update make a model retyping prose a silent-corruption risk |
| Project **field** values are not settable with plain `gh issue` commands | `gh project item-edit` needs the item id, not the issue number. If a field must change, say so rather than claiming it done |
| Labels mirroring a field are not the same as the field | `gh issue list --label mod:x` is the cheap query; the field is what board views group by. Keep them in step at creation, and read the **field** for collision checks |
